claim: The intestinal microbiota critically influences a multitude of host physiological functions, often through modulation of the immune system.
source: The intestinal microbiota has been shown to critically influence a multitude of host physiological functions, often through modulation of the immune system (Gevers et al., 2014; Paun et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Gevers et al., 2014; Paun et al., 2016).

claim: Both pro-inflammatory T-helper 17 (Th17) cells and anti-inflammatory regulatory T-cells (Treg) are reduced in numbers in the intestinal lamina propria of germ-free mice relative to conventional or specific pathogen-free mice.
source: Evidence includes studies in germ-free mice, which show that both pro-inflammatory T-helper 17 (Th17) cells and anti-inflammatory regulatory T-cells (Treg) are reduced in numbers in the intestinal lamina propria relative to conventional or specific pathogen-free mice (Atarashi et al., 2008)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Atarashi et al., 2008).

claim: Repopulation of germ-free mice with specific bacteria can reconstitute Th17 cells and Treg.
source: repopulation with specific bacteria can reconstitute them (Atarashi et al., 2015; Ivanov et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Atarashi et al., 2015; Ivanov et al., 2009).

claim: The microbiota influences immune system activation through the production of small molecules.
source: One route to how the microbiota influences immune system activation is by the production of small molecules (Donia and Fischbach, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Donia and Fischbach, 2015).

claim: Microbially produced short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) facilitate extrathymic differentiation of immune system modulatory Treg.
source: Microbially produced short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) were shown to facilitate extrathymic differentiation of immune system modulatory Treg (Arpaia et al., 2013; Atarashi et al., 2013; Smith et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Arpaia et al., 2013; Atarashi et al., 2013; Smith et al., 2013).

claim: SCFAs are implicated in Treg-dependent anti-inflammatory properties of a mix of 17 human-derived Clostridia strains.
source: are implicated in Treg-dependent anti-inflammatory properties of a mix of 17 human-derived Clostridia strains (Atarashi et al., 2013; Tanoue et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Atarashi et al., 2013; Tanoue et al., 2016).

claim: Individual Clostridia strains only have a modest effect on Treg induction.
source: Interestingly, individual Clostridia strains only have a modest effect on Treg induction – optimal induction relies on the synergistic interplay of several strains (Atarashi et al., 2013; Belkaid and Hand, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Atarashi et al., 2013; Belkaid and Hand, 2014).

claim: Optimal Treg induction relies on the synergistic interplay of several Clostridia strains.
source: Interestingly, individual Clostridia strains only have a modest effect on Treg induction – optimal induction relies on the synergistic interplay of several strains (Atarashi et al., 2013; Belkaid and Hand, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Atarashi et al., 2013; Belkaid and Hand, 2014).

claim: There is great interest in the manipulation of the Clostridia community for the treatment of inflammatory and allergic diseases.
source: Because of these properties, there is currently great interest in the manipulation of this community for the treatment of inflammatory and allergic diseases (Honda and Littman, 2012; Olle, 2013; Vieira et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Honda and Littman, 2012; Olle, 2013; Vieira et al., 2016).

claim: Microbiota repopulation from healthy humans to humans with C. difficile infections has provided evidence that it could be used as a strategy for disease prevention and treatment.
source: Efforts involving transplantation of bacteria from healthy humans to humans with C. difficile infections or with metabolic diseases have provided evidence that microbiota repopulation could be used as possible strategy for disease prevention and treatment (van Nood et al., 2013; Vrieze et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (van Nood et al., 2013; Vrieze et al., 2012).

claim: Microbiota repopulation from healthy humans to humans with metabolic diseases has provided evidence that it could be used as a strategy for disease prevention and treatment.
source: Efforts involving transplantation of bacteria from healthy humans to humans with C. difficile infections or with metabolic diseases have provided evidence that microbiota repopulation could be used as possible strategy for disease prevention and treatment (van Nood et al., 2013; Vrieze et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (van Nood et al., 2013; Vrieze et al., 2012).

claim: Intestinal supplementation of defined compositions of gut bacteria to treat a range of diseases is currently being pursued by multiple bio-pharmaceutical companies.
source: For this reason, intestinal supplementation of defined compositions of gut bacteria to treat a range of diseases is currently being pursued by multiple bio-pharmaceutical companies (Garber, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Garber, 2015).

claim: Determining what microbial consortia can colonize the host and stably coexist with an already resident microbial community, while inducing the desired immune response, is a major challenge that hinders translation into the clinic.
source: Determining what microbial consortia can colonize the host and stably coexist with an already resident microbial community, while inducing the desired immune response, is still a major challenge that hinders the translation of these efforts into the clinic (Maldonado-Gómez et al., 2016; Weil and Hohmann, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Maldonado-Gómez et al., 2016; Weil and Hohmann, 2015).

claim: A set of 17 potent Treg-inducing Clostridia strains was previously identified.
source: In previous work, some of us identified a set of 17 potent Treg-inducing Clostridia strains to select candidate subsets from (Atarashi et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Atarashi et al., 2013).

claim: Testing all possible subsets of 17 strains would require testing 131,071 combinations in mice, which is experimentally infeasible.
source: The determination of maximally immune-phenotype inducing combinations from these 17 strains is, however, experimentally infeasible as it would require the testing of 217–1 = 131071 possible subsets in mice (Faith et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by mathematical calculation and a citation (Faith et al., 2014).

claim: A computational approach to prioritize which subsets to validate experimentally would have great utility.
source: Therefore, a computational approach to prioritize which subsets to validate experimentally would have great utility.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the infeasibility of testing all combinations.

claim: To date there has been no model that allows for the simultaneous prediction of the dynamics of both the microbiota and the host immune response.
source: To our knowledge, to date there has been no model that allows for the simultaneous prediction of the dynamics of both the microbiota and the host immune response.
evidence: This is a statement of the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The study proposes a mathematical modeling-based framework that allows computational optimization of immune-stimulating bacterial combinations.
source: we overcome this problem by proposing a mathematical modeling-based framework that, by resolving microbiome–immune system interactions with parameters constrained to experimental observations of microbiome and immune effectors, allows computational optimization of immune-stimulating bacterial combinations.
evidence: This is a description of the work presented in the manuscript.

claim: The study uses a series of logically connected analyses that capture CD4+FOXP3+ Treg accumulation in the colonic lamina propria in response to the dynamics of human-derived Clostridia strains in germ-free mice.
source: To achieve this, we use a series of logically connected analyses that capture CD4+FOXP3+ Treg accumulation in the colonic lamina propria (Omenetti and Pizarro, 2015; Round and Mazmanian, 2010) in response to the dynamics of human-derived Clostridia strains in germ-free mice, which had previously been shown to potently induce Treg expansion (Atarashi et al., 2013) (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a description of the methodology with supporting citations (Omenetti and Pizarro, 2015; Round and Mazmanian, 2010; Atarashi et al., 2013).

claim: The study combines previously published and newly generated FACS data with simulated and newly generated time-series colonization data from germ-free mice.
source: To constrain this proposed model framework to experimental data, we combine previously published (Atarashi et al., 2013) and newly generated fluorescence-activated cell scanning (FACS) data with simulated and newly generated time-series colonization data from germ-free mice (Figure 2A).
evidence: This describes the data sources used in the study, referencing both published data (Atarashi et al., 2013) and newly generated data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The study infers each strain's individual contribution to the CD4+FOXP3+ Treg pool by applying a microbiome–Treg mathematical model.
source: Subsequently, by applying a microbiome–Treg mathematical model to this combined data set, we infer each strain's individual contribution to the CD4+FOXP3+ Treg pool (Figure 2B)
evidence: This describes the analytical approach and references Figure 2B showing the results.

claim: The study validates the microbiome ecological model's ability to predict temporal dynamics in response to different subsets of Treg-inducing strains.
source: To justify the usage of predicted mono-colonization concentrations from a previously developed microbiome ecological model (Bucci et al., 2016), we validate its ability in predicting temporal dynamics in response to different subsets of Treg-inducing strains (Figure 3A) and quantify the deviation of data and predictions (Figure 3B).
evidence: This describes validation experiments with results shown in Figures 3A and 3B, referencing a previously published model (Bucci et al., 2016).

claim: The TrIS assigns a score to every predicted steady-state microbial composition.
source: Introduction of the TrIS, which assigns a score to every predicted steady-state microbial composition, enables us to identify combinations that robustly maximize Treg induction (Figure 4A).
evidence: This describes the TrIS metric introduced in the study, with results shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The study demonstrates the utility of the approach in predicting the potency of selected microbial combinations by validating Treg induction and colonization ability of model-predicted strong, intermediate and weak Treg-inducing consortia in vivo.
source: Most importantly, we demonstrate the utility of our approach in predicting the potency of selected microbial combinations by validating the Treg induction and colonization ability of model-predicted strong, intermediate and weak Treg-inducing consortia in vivo (Figure 4E).
evidence: This describes validation experiments with results shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The framework may have direct relevance to other immune-system enhancing applications such as the optimal delivery of probiotic-based cancer immunotherapies.
source: We envision that our framework, while in this study tailored to finding combinations ameliorating auto-inflammatory conditions, may also have direct relevance to other immune-system enhancing applications such as the optimal delivery of probiotic-based cancer immunotherapies (Garrett, 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential applications, supported by a citation (Garrett, 2015).

claim: The study uses 12 Treg-inducing Clostridia strains that are part of an original consortium of 17 Treg-inducing strains.
source: For (i), we gathered newly produced quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) colonization data from gnotobiotic mice and combined it with a previously published microbiome ecological model of the dynamics of 12 Treg-inducing Clostridia strains that are part of an original consortium of 17 Treg-inducing strains discovered by some of us (Atarashi et al., 2013) (see also Table 1 for a breakdown of strains used in each study).
evidence: This describes the strains used in the study, referencing published work (Atarashi et al., 2013) and Table 1.

claim: Strain 6 from the 13-strain set was predicted to not stably colonize in the presence of the other 12 strains.
source: In contrast to the original study of (Bucci et al., 2016), we included only 12 of the 13 strains used there because, based on the modeling and analysis of Bucci et al. (2016), Strain 6 from the 13-strain set was predicted to not stably colonize in the presence of the other 12 strains.
evidence: This is based on modeling predictions from a previous study (Bucci et al., 2016).

claim: The published colonization data include time-series measurements of microbial abundances by qPCR under dietary perturbations.
source: The published colonization data have been reported in our previous work (Bucci et al., 2016) and include time-series measurements of microbial abundances by qPCR under dietary perturbations.
evidence: This describes data from a previous publication (Bucci et al., 2016).

claim: The colonization data are used to derive a predictive microbiome ecology model based on an extension of the generalized Lotka–Volterra equations.
source: These are used to derive a predictive microbiome ecology model in gnotobiotic conditions based on an extension of the generalized Lotka–Volterra (gLV) equations (Hofbauer and Sigmund, 1998) as introduced in Stein et al. (2013).
evidence: This describes the modeling approach with citations to foundational work (Hofbauer and Sigmund, 1998; Stein et al., 2013).

claim: 14 mice were gavaged with one of three possible 11-strain subsets from the 12-strain subset.
source: For the newly generated dataset, we gavaged 14 mice with one of three possible 11-strain subsets from the 12-strain subset of original 13 strains (Figure 2)
evidence: This describes the experimental design with reference to Figure 2.

claim: The three 11-strain subsets were chosen based on the 'keystoneness' definition.
source: The three 11-strain subsets were chosen based on our 'keystoneness' definition, a measure describing the marginal predicted quantitative effect of removing each strain from the full community (Bucci et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes the selection criteria with reference to a previous publication (Bucci et al., 2016).

claim: Two 11-strain combinations each missing one of the two highest keystoneness-scoring strains (VE202 Strain 15 and VE202 Strain 4) were included.
source: Specifically, we included two 11-strain combinations each missing one of the two highest keystoneness-scoring strains (VE202 Strain 15 and VE202 Strain 4) and one 11-strain combination which lacks the lowest keystoneness scoring strain (VE202 Strain 29).
evidence: This describes the specific strain combinations used in the experiments.

claim: One 11-strain combination lacks the lowest keystoneness scoring strain (VE202 Strain 29).
source: Specifically, we included two 11-strain combinations each missing one of the two highest keystoneness-scoring strains (VE202 Strain 15 and VE202 Strain 4) and one 11-strain combination which lacks the lowest keystoneness scoring strain (VE202 Strain 29).
evidence: This describes the specific strain combinations used in the experiments.

claim: Each strain's density was profiled over time by qPCR with strain-specific primers.
source: In analogy to Bucci et al. (2016), each strain's density was profiled over time by qPCR with strain-specific primers (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology with reference to a previous publication (Bucci et al., 2016).

claim: The colonization data from fecal content was coupled with newly collected and published FACS measurements of the CD4+FOXP3+ Treg population in the lamina propria.
source: To resolve the contribution of each of these to Treg induction for point (ii) we coupled the colonization data from fecal content with newly collected and published FACS measurements of the CD4+FOXP3+ Treg population in the lamina propria of these mice (Figure 2A).
evidence: This describes the data integration approach with reference to Figure 2A.

claim: CD4+FOXP3+ Treg measurements from previously published mono-colonization experiments were included.
source: As it is crucial to capture each strain's contribution alone and in combination with others, we also included CD4+FOXP3+ Treg measurements from our previously published mono-colonization experiments (Atarashi et al., 2013) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This describes the inclusion of previously published data (Atarashi et al., 2013) shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Single-strain mono-colonization concentrations were not measured in the previous mono-colonization experiments.
source: Due to the fact that the single-strain mono-colonization concentrations were not measured in these experiments (Atarashi et al., 2013), we simulated them using the microbiome ecological model and parameters from (Bucci et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes a limitation of the previous data (Atarashi et al., 2013) and the approach taken to address it using the model from (Bucci et al., 2016).

claim: The model's capability in predicting unseen validation data supports the use of simulated mono-colonization concentrations.
source: This choice was supported by the model's capability in predicting unseen validation data (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a justification based on model validation results shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Spearman's rank-order correlation coefficient ranges from 0.92 to 0.98 (p-value<10−16) between observations and predictions depending on the time point.
source: Spearman's rank-order correlation coefficient ranges from 0.92 to 0.98 (p-value<10−16) between observations and predictions depending on the time point (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the validation analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The population of CD4+ T-cells is subdivided into two major subpopulations: CD4+FOXP3+ Treg and CD4+FOXP3− T-cells.
source: We begin by subdividing the population of CD4+ T-cells into two major subpopulations depending on their intracellular FOXP3 expression: CD4+FOXP3+ Treg and the remainder among the CD4+ T-cells, the conventional CD4+FOXP3− T-cells (Bilate and Lafaille, 2012; Rudensky, 2011).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge in immunology, supported by citations (Bilate and Lafaille, 2012; Rudensky, 2011).

claim: T-cell dynamics are assumed to follow the generalized Lotka–Volterra equations.
source: To include a variety of effects into our model, we assume T-cell dynamics to follow the gLV equations (Gerber, 2014; Hofbauer and Sigmund, 1998)
evidence: This describes a modeling assumption with supporting citations (Gerber, 2014; Hofbauer and Sigmund, 1998).

claim: The study uses an extension of the standard gLV equations to include the impact of the Clostridia strains in terms of external perturbations.
source: In addition, we use an extension of the standard gLV equations to include the impact of the Clostridia strains in terms of external perturbations (Stein et al., 2013).
evidence: This describes a modeling approach with a citation (Stein et al., 2013).

claim: The assumption of constant steady-state CD4+ T-cell concentration is justified because the study deals with genetically similar mice and a set of closely related Clostridia.
source: We justify this because we are dealing with genetically similar mice and a set of closely related Clostridia.
evidence: This is a justification for the modeling assumption based on the experimental design.

claim: The assumption of constant steady-state CD4+ T-cell concentration is not justifiable when comparing non-colonized and colonized germ-free mice.
source: This assumption is however not justifiable when comparing non-colonized and colonized germ-free mice (Faith et al., 2014).
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation of the assumption with a citation (Faith et al., 2014).

claim: The resulting normalized root-mean square deviation on left-out samples was found to be 12%.
source: The resulting normalized root-mean square deviation on left-out samples was found to be 12%.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the cross-validation analysis.

claim: Of the 4095 possible steady-state strain configurations evaluated, 84% are found to be biologically meaningful and stable.
source: In our computation, of the 212–1 = 4095 possible steady-state strain configurations evaluated in N = 22,500 MCMC parameter estimates, 84% are found to be biologically meaningful and stable.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the computational analysis.

claim: While the average TrIS increases with consortium size, a subset size of seven already contains bacterial combinations maximizing induction.
source: Interestingly, while the average TrIS increases with consortium size, our analysis shows that a subset size of seven already contains bacterial combinations maximizing induction (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: There is a strong correlation between TrIS and the predicted total bacterial abundance in the consortium.
source: Furthermore, in addition to the strong correlation between TrIS and the predicted total bacterial abundance in the consortium, we observed that high-induction consortia display an especially large enrichment in the abundance of Strain 27 (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: High-induction consortia display an especially large enrichment in the abundance of Strain 27.
source: Furthermore, in addition to the strong correlation between TrIS and the predicted total bacterial abundance in the consortium, we observed that high-induction consortia display an especially large enrichment in the abundance of Strain 27 (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Short-chain fatty acids have been previously associated with colonic Treg induction.
source: Because short-chain fatty acids have been previously associated with colonic Treg induction (Arpaia et al., 2013)
evidence: This is based on previous research with a citation (Arpaia et al., 2013).

claim: SCFAs increase in density upon supplementation with these Clostridia strains.
source: and increase in density upon supplementation with these strains (Atarashi et al., 2013)
evidence: This is based on previous research with a citation (Atarashi et al., 2013).

claim: The top 5-inducing microbial consortia of size seven were compared against their bottom 5 counterparts for SCFA enrichment.
source: We therefore compared the top 5-inducing microbial consortia of size seven against their same-size counterpart bottom 5 (Figure 4C).
evidence: This describes the comparative analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The SCFA concentration for each predicted composition was predicted by summing the scaled metabolic outputs of each strain measured in mono-colonization experiments.
source: We predicted the SCFA concentration for each of the predicted compositions by summing the scaled metabolic outputs of each strain measured in mono-colonization experiments (Atarashi et al., 2013; Narushima et al., 2014) and normalized by the strain's model-predicted mono-colonization density.
evidence: This describes the method for predicting SCFA concentrations using data from previous publications (Atarashi et al., 2013; Narushima et al., 2014).

claim: Significant enrichment for all estimated SCFAs (p<0.05, one tailed) was found in the high-TrIS consortia compared to the low ones.
source: We performed a Welch two-samples t-test for each of the predicted SCFAs concentrations and found significant enrichment for all estimated SCFAs (p<0.05, one tailed) in the high-TrIS consortia compared to the low ones (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Five 4-strain combinations with a variety of predicted immune effects were selected for experimental testing.
source: Due to regulatory constraints on the used probiotic strains – limiting us to a maximum of four strains at a time in follow-up experiments – we selected five 4-strain combinations with a variety of predicted immune effects.
evidence: This describes the experimental design for validation.

claim: CD4+FOXP3+ Treg induction was measured for five microbial consortia of size four and the germ-free control.
source: We measured CD4+FOXP3+ Treg induction for five microbial consortia of size four and the germ-free control.
evidence: This describes the experimental measurements performed.

claim: The two highest TrIS consortia (H1 and H2 with rank 1 and 2, respectively), the lowest one (L with rank 495) and two TrIS-intermediate consortia (M1, M2 with rank 129 and 452, respectively) were chosen for validation.
source: We chose the two highest TrIS consortia (H1, H2 with rank 1 and 2, respectively), the lowest one (L with rank 495) and two TrIS-intermediate consortia of interest (M1, M2 with rank 129 and 452, respectively).
evidence: This describes the specific consortia selected for validation.

claim: A significant Pearson correlation with coefficient of 0.97 and p-value<0.01 was found between the TrIS score and the mean observed CD4+FOXP3+ Treg percentage.
source: We correlated the TrIS score with the mean observed CD4+FOXP3+ Treg percentage and found a significant Pearson correlation with coefficient of 0.97 and p-value<0.01 (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the validation experiment shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The high TrIS-scoring consortia (H1, H2, M1) all stably colonized while the two low-scoring consortia only displayed a subset of the introduced strains.
source: Importantly, when using 16S rRNA sequencing to investigate the resulting colonization profiles for these combinations, we observed that the high TrIS-scoring consortia (H1, H2, M1) all stably colonized while the two low-scoring consortia only displayed a subset of the introduced strains.
evidence: This is a finding from the colonization profiling experiments.

claim: The H2 consortium displays an average increase in immune activity of 107% relative to the average germ-free mouse control.
source: Importantly, the H2 consortium displays an average increase in immune activity of 107% relative to the average germ-free mouse control.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the validation experiment.

claim: ANOVA and subsequent post-hoc Tukey test showed significance in the measured enrichment of H1 compared to L (adjusted p-value<0.05) for acetic acid concentrations.
source: ANOVA and subsequent post-hoc Tukey test showed significance in the measured enrichment of H1 compared to L (adjusted p-value<0.05) and of H1 compared to H2 (adjusted p-value<0.05) (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the metabolic profiling analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: ANOVA and subsequent post-hoc Tukey test showed significance in the measured enrichment of H1 compared to H2 (adjusted p-value<0.05) for acetic acid concentrations.
source: ANOVA and subsequent post-hoc Tukey test showed significance in the measured enrichment of H1 compared to L (adjusted p-value<0.05) and of H1 compared to H2 (adjusted p-value<0.05) (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the metabolic profiling analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: No statistical difference was observed between measurements in H2 and L for acetic acid concentrations (adjusted p-value<0.05).
source: However, no statistical difference was observed between measurements in H2 and L (adjusted p-value<0.05).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the metabolic profiling analysis.

claim: The model-predicted germ-free normalized acetate enrichment and the observed acetic acid concentration are well correlated.
source: Remarkably, the model-predicted germ-free normalized acetate enrichment and the observed acetic acid concentration (normalized by the mean in germ-free conditions) are well correlated (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is a finding from the comparison of predicted and observed metabolite concentrations shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Choosing bacterial combinations from the vast combinatorial space of microbes that effectively colonize a host and maximize a desired host phenotype requires an enormous number of expensive and time-consuming experimental trials.
source: However, choosing bacterial combinations from the vast combinatorial space of microbes that effectively colonize a host (possibly with a dysbiotic microbiota) and at the same time maximize a desired host phenotype requires an enormous number of expensive and time-consuming experimental trials (Faith et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement about the challenge in the field, supported by a citation (Faith et al., 2014).

claim: The majority of available microbiome analysis methods is still based on correlations and inept at predicting unseen phenotypes.
source: While data mining and statistical approaches could aid in this process, the majority of available microbiome analysis methods is still based on correlations (Gerber, 2014; Morgan et al., 2015) and inept at predicting unseen phenotypes.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of current methods, supported by citations (Gerber, 2014; Morgan et al., 2015).

claim: Identification of causal associations between microbes and host phenotype has been recently achieved by using an experimentally based microbe–phenotype triangulation.
source: Identification of causal associations between microbes and host phenotype has been recently achieved by using an experimentally based microbe–phenotype triangulation (Surana and Kasper, 2017).
evidence: This is based on recent research with a citation (Surana and Kasper, 2017).

claim: The microbe-phenotype triangulation approach remains impractical when the goal is to explore and rank all possible microbiome consortium combinations with respect to a host phenotype of interest.
source: However, this approach remains impractical when the goal is to explore and rank all possible microbiome consortium combinations with respect to a host phenotype of interest.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the limitations of the triangulation approach.

claim: The study leveraged previous computational methods to forecast temporal microbiome dynamics and make predictions on stability in the context of infectious and inflammatory diseases.
source: In this study, we leveraged our previous computational methods to forecast temporal microbiome dynamics and make predictions on stability in the context of infectious and inflammatory diseases including C. difficile colonization and inflammatory bowel disease (Bucci et al., 2016; Buffie et al., 2015; Stein et al., 2013).
evidence: This describes the foundation of the current work with citations to previous publications (Bucci et al., 2016; Buffie et al., 2015; Stein et al., 2013).

claim: The study presents a novel modeling-based method that combines dynamical predictions from data-driven models of the microbiome and the interactions between microbes and the immune response.
source: Specifically, we have presented a novel modeling-based method that combines dynamical predictions from data-driven models of the microbiome and the interactions between microbes and the immune response (such as CD4+FOXP3+ Treg) and thereby enables the rational design of immune-modulating bacterial consortia.
evidence: This is a summary of the main contribution of the study.

claim: The proposed framework is naturally extensible to other host data, for example data from metabolite profiling, immune readouts, or host transcriptome profiling.
source: However, the proposed framework is naturally extensible to other host data, for example data from metabolite profiling, immune readouts (e.g. CD8 T-cell activation, Th1/Th17 cell depletion) or host transcriptome profiling (Atarashi et al., 2017; Morgan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a statement about the potential extensibility of the framework, with citations (Atarashi et al., 2017; Morgan et al., 2015).

claim: This is the first study in which observation-constrained in silico modeling of microbiome and host phenotype has successfully guided the rational design of drugs of defined bacterial consortia.
source: To our knowledge, this is to date, the first study in which observation-constrained in silico modeling of microbiome and host phenotype has successfully guided the rational design of drugs of defined bacterial consortia.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty and significance of the work.

claim: The gLV model assumption has limitations including the lack of third or higher order interactions or saturation effects.
source: Our work relies on the gLV model assumption for both microbiome and CD4+ regulatory T-cell dynamics which, despite being very versatile, has some limitations including the lack of third or higher order interactions or saturation effects (Wangersky, 1978).
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation of the modeling approach with a citation (Wangersky, 1978).

claim: The assumption that the overall T-cell density at steady state is constant across mice and different microbiome compositions was necessary with the available data.
source: Moreover, with the data available to us, we needed to assume that the overall T-cell density at steady state is constant across mice and different microbiome compositions.
evidence: This acknowledges a modeling assumption necessitated by data limitations.

claim: The addition of future measurements on total T-cell abundance will likely improve the prediction accuracy of the model.
source: While this assumption was reasonable for the data we analyzed (see Results), the addition of future measurements on total T-cell abundance will likely improve the prediction accuracy of our model as well as provide important insight into the variability of T-cell population size in response to microbial immune induction.
evidence: This is a speculation about how future data could improve the model.

claim: Previous work showed that the amount of Treg induction is independent of the germ-free background (IQI, Balb/c or C57BL/6).
source: While previous work by some of us showed that the amount of Treg induction is independent of the germ-free background (IQI, Balb/c or C57BL/6) (Atarashi et al., 2015)
evidence: This is based on previous research with a citation (Atarashi et al., 2015).

claim: The model, which was trained on IQI mice data, robustly predicted both Treg induction and acetate enrichment of C57BL/6 colonized mice used in the validation experiments.
source: it is noteworthy that our model, which was trained on IQI mice data, robustly predicted both Treg induction and acetate enrichment of C57BL/6 colonized mice as used in the validation experiments.
evidence: This is a finding from the validation experiments.

claim: The predictions suggest some degree of consistency in terms of functional outcome (e.g. enrichment in acetate) of high-scoring consortia relative to low-scoring ones in germ-free mice.
source: Our predictions suggest some degree of consistency in terms of functional outcome (e.g. enrichment in acetate) of high-scoring consortia relative to low-scoring ones in germ-free mice.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the analysis.

claim: Before translating these findings into therapeutic development, future studies will need to be performed in not germ-free settings.
source: However, before translating these findings into therapeutic development, future studies will need to be performed in not germ-free settings (e.g. SPF mice, humanized mice) in order to account for the effects of an already-established flora.
evidence: This is a statement about the need for future work before clinical translation.
